course.title: AWS Cloud Practitioner Capstone
course.description: Build a small company in AWS in four weeks: a VPC, an instance, a website with HTTPS and a serverless counter — then watch it run.
course.audience: Four roles build a real AWS environment in four weeks, on a $5 budget. Start here.

roles.mission: Owns the design, the standards, the cost and each week’s document.
roles.label: 📐 Cloud Architect

roles.name: Infrastructure Admin
roles.mission: Builds the network, the VM, the data and the templates.
roles.label: 🧱 Infrastructure Admin

roles.name: App & DevOps
roles.mission: Ships the website, the API and the pipeline.
roles.label: 🚀 App & DevOps

roles.name: Security & Ops
roles.mission: Locks access down, watches it run, and works the incidents.
roles.label: 🛡️ Security & Ops

tasks.title: Set the naming standard and the budget
tasks.objective: Agree how everything is named and tagged, and cap spending at $5 before anything is built.
definitionOfDone: The naming and tag table is agreed

steps.title: Create the $5 budget
steps.description: The budget capstone-team01 is listed with a $5 amount and alerts at 85% and 100%.
steps.where: AWS console — Billing and Cost Management → Budgets
steps.instruction: Create a $5 monthly budget that emails the team.
instructionList: Create budget → Use a template → Monthly cost budget.
Name: capstone-team01. Amount: 5.
Email recipients: the team email. Create.
steps.expectedOutput: The budget capstone-team01 is listed with a $5 amount and alerts at 85% and 100%.
steps.whatItMeans: The budget is the guardrail. It is created first because it is the one thing that tells you a mistake is costing money.

fixes.fix: Sign in as the root user once and enable IAM access to billing (Account → IAM user access to billing).

steps.title: Agree the naming and tags
steps.description: A table of prefixes and four tag keys everyone has agreed to use.
steps.instruction: Agree one naming pattern and four tags as a team.
instructionList: Pattern: type prefix, workload, team — e.g. ec2-tools-team01.
Prefixes: vpc-, snet-, rt-, igw-, sg-, ec2-, ebs-; buckets and functions start capstone-team01-.
Tags: project, team, env, owner.
steps.expectedOutput: A table of prefixes and four tag keys everyone has agreed to use.
steps.whatItMeans: AWS resource names are mostly free text; the Name tag and a pattern are what make them readable. Week 11 checks the owner tag.

steps.title: Record it in the Cloud Foundation & Naming Standard
steps.description: Your section: Account and guardrails, Naming, Tags, RACI.
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Cloud Foundation & Naming Standard.
instructionList: Account alias, region (us-east-1) and the budget.
One naming row per resource type you will create.
The four tags, and a short RACI.

tasks.title: Create the VPC and public subnet
tasks.objective: Create a VPC with one public subnet, an internet gateway and a route, named and tagged by the standard.
definitionOfDone: The public subnet routes 0.0.0.0/0 to the IGW

steps.title: Create the VPC and subnet
steps.instruction: Create the VPC 10.10.0.0/16 and subnet 10.10.1.0/24.

commands.cmd: TAGS="{Key=project,Value=capstone},{Key=team,Value=team01},{Key=owner,Value=team01-infra}"; VPC=$(aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.10.0.0/16 --tag-specifications "ResourceType=vpc,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=vpc-capstone-team01},$TAGS]" --query Vpc.VpcId --output text); echo $VPC
commands.explain: The VPC is your private network. Its id is kept in $VPC for the next lines.

commands.cmd: SUB=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id $VPC --cidr-block 10.10.1.0/24 --availability-zone us-east-1a --tag-specifications "ResourceType=subnet,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=snet-public-team01},$TAGS]" --query Subnet.SubnetId --output text); echo $SUB
commands.explain: A subnet lives in exactly one Availability Zone.

steps.whatItMeans: A /16 leaves room for 256 /24 subnets; the course uses two. Private ranges never route on the internet.

steps.title: Give it a way out
steps.instruction: Add an internet gateway and a default route.

commands.cmd: IGW=$(aws ec2 create-internet-gateway --query InternetGateway.InternetGatewayId --output text); aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --internet-gateway-id $IGW --vpc-id $VPC
commands.explain: The internet gateway is the VPC’s door to the internet.

commands.cmd: RT=$(aws ec2 create-route-table --vpc-id $VPC --query RouteTable.RouteTableId --output text); aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id $RT --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --gateway-id $IGW; aws ec2 associate-route-table --route-table-id $RT --subnet-id $SUB --query AssociationState.State --output text
commands.explain: A subnet is "public" only because its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the gateway.

steps.whatItMeans: Public or private is a routing decision, not a setting on the subnet.

fixes.fix: CloudShell restarted. Look the id up: aws ec2 describe-vpcs --filters Name=tag:Name,Values=vpc-capstone-team01.

steps.title: Record it in the Cloud Foundation & Naming Standard
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Cloud Foundation & Naming Standard.
instructionList: The VPC and subnet names.
The address space and the first subnet.
steps.whatItMeans: The Network Design Document in Week 6 starts from these numbers.

tasks.title: Create the security group
tasks.objective: Create the tools security group with no inbound rules, and review who has access to the account.

steps.title: Create the security group
steps.instruction: Create sg-tools-team01 in the VPC.

commands.cmd: VPC=$(aws ec2 describe-vpcs --filters Name=tag:Name,Values=vpc-capstone-team01 --query "Vpcs[0].VpcId" --output text); SG=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name sg-tools-team01 --description "Tools instance" --vpc-id $VPC --query GroupId --output text); echo $SG
commands.explain: A security group is a stateful firewall around an instance. It starts by allowing nothing in.

steps.whatItMeans: Security groups are allow-only: there is no deny rule, only the absence of an allow.

steps.title: Read its rules
steps.instruction: List inbound and outbound rules.

commands.cmd: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --group-ids $SG --query "SecurityGroups[0].{inbound:IpPermissions, outbound:IpPermissionsEgress[0].IpRanges}"
commands.explain: Inbound is empty; outbound allows everything, which is the default.

steps.whatItMeans: Knowing the defaults is how you know every rule you add is a decision.

steps.title: Review access (IAM)
steps.description: A list of users, their groups and MFA status.
steps.instruction: List who can sign in and with what.
instructionList: IAM → Users: note each user, group and MFA status.
Confirm the root user has MFA and no access keys.
steps.expectedOutput: A list of users, their groups and MFA status.
steps.whatItMeans: Least privilege starts with knowing what is granted today. Week 5 narrows it.

steps.title: Price it

instructionList: Context: a public site with HTTPS for under $1 a month.
Decision: private S3 bucket behind CloudFront with Origin Access Control.

steps.expectedOutput: ADR-001 with context, decision, rejected options and consequences.

tasks.title: Launch the tools instance
tasks.objective: Launch a t3.micro Amazon Linux instance in the public subnet with a key pair and IMDSv2, then stop it.
definitionOfDone: ec2-tools-team01 runs in the public subnet
The instance is stopped at the end

steps.title: Launch the instance
steps.instruction: Launch the t3.micro with IMDSv2 required.

commands.cmd: aws ec2 create-key-pair --key-name kp-team01 --query KeyMaterial --output text > kp-team01.pem && chmod 400 kp-team01.pem
commands.explain: The private key is shown once. Download it from CloudShell (Actions → Download) and never commit it.

commands.cmd: SUB=$(aws ec2 describe-subnets --filters Name=tag:Name,Values=snet-public-team01 --query "Subnets[0].SubnetId" --output text); SG=$(aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters Name=group-name,Values=sg-tools-team01 --query "SecurityGroups[0].GroupId" --output text); aws ec2 run-instances --image-id resolve:ssm:/aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64 --instance-type t3.micro --key-name kp-team01 --subnet-id $SUB --security-group-ids $SG --associate-public-ip-address --metadata-options HttpTokens=required --tag-specifications "ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=ec2-tools-team01},{Key=owner,Value=team01-infra}]" --query "Instances[0].{id:InstanceId, ip:PrivateIpAddress}"
commands.explain: resolve:ssm always picks the current Amazon Linux image. HttpTokens=required turns on IMDSv2, which blocks a common credential-theft trick.

steps.whatItMeans: t3.micro is free-tier eligible. IMDSv2 is off by default on older launch paths — always require it.

fixes.fix: Your account’s free tier is t2.micro. Use --instance-type t2.micro and record why.

steps.title: Read its network facts
steps.instruction: Read the private and public IPs.

commands.cmd: IID=$(aws ec2 describe-instances --filters Name=tag:Name,Values=ec2-tools-team01 Name=instance-state-name,Values=running,stopped --query "Reservations[0].Instances[0].InstanceId" --output text); aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids $IID --query "Reservations[0].Instances[0].{private:PrivateIpAddress, public:PublicIpAddress, state:State.Name}"
commands.explain: The private IP is what other resources use; the public IP only exists for outbound patching and your SSH test.

steps.whatItMeans: AWS reserves the first four addresses and the last in every subnet.

steps.title: Record it in the Solution Architecture Document
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Solution Architecture Document.
instructionList: Name, type, private IP, operating system.
steps.whatItMeans: The runbook in Week 7 and the snapshot in Week 8 start from these facts.

steps.title: Stop the instance
steps.instruction: Stop the instance so it stops costing money.

commands.cmd: IID=$(aws ec2 describe-instances --filters Name=tag:Name,Values=ec2-tools-team01 Name=instance-state-name,Values=running,stopped --query "Reservations[0].Instances[0].InstanceId" --output text); aws ec2 stop-instances --instance-ids $IID --query "StoppingInstances[0].CurrentState.Name" --output text
commands.explain: A stopped instance pays only for its disk. Stopping from inside the OS does the same; forgetting does not.

commands.cmd: aws ec2 wait instance-stopped --instance-ids $IID && echo stopped
commands.explain: Waits until it is fully stopped.

steps.whatItMeans: A running t3.micro costs about 1 cent an hour; a forgotten one eats the budget in weeks.

tasks.title: Publish the website with CloudFront
tasks.objective: Publish the site from a private S3 bucket behind CloudFront with Origin Access Control, then change it and redeploy.

steps.title: Create the bucket and upload
steps.instruction: Create a private bucket and upload the site.

commands.cmd: BUCKET=capstone-team01-site-$RANDOM; aws s3 mb s3://$BUCKET && aws s3 sync ./site s3://$BUCKET
commands.explain: Bucket names are global. Block Public Access is on by default — leave it on; CloudFront will read the bucket for you.

steps.whatItMeans: The bucket never becomes public. That is the difference from the old S3-website approach.

steps.title: Put CloudFront in front
steps.description: The distribution is Enabled and https://d….cloudfront.net shows your page.
steps.instruction: Create a distribution with Origin Access Control.
instructionList: Origin: your bucket (not the website endpoint). Origin access: Origin access control settings → Create.
Viewer protocol policy: Redirect HTTP to HTTPS. Default root object: index.html.
Create, then Copy policy and paste it into the bucket’s Permissions → Bucket policy.
steps.expectedOutput: The distribution is Enabled and https://d….cloudfront.net shows your page.
steps.whatItMeans: OAC signs CloudFront’s requests; the bucket policy admits only this distribution. Deployment takes about five minutes.

fixes.fix: The bucket policy was not pasted, or the origin is the website endpoint instead of the bucket.

steps.title: Redeploy a change
steps.instruction: Upload a change and clear the cache.

commands.cmd: aws s3 sync ./site s3://$BUCKET && DIST=$(aws cloudfront list-distributions --query "DistributionList.Items[0].Id" --output text) && aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id $DIST --paths "/*" --query Invalidation.Status --output text
commands.explain: CloudFront caches; an invalidation tells it to fetch the new files.

steps.whatItMeans: Upload plus invalidate is a redeploy. Week 10 automates it.

steps.title: Record it in the Solution Architecture Document
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Solution Architecture Document.
instructionList: The HTTPS URL.
How you redeployed a change.
steps.whatItMeans: The CloudFront URL is the origin CORS will admit in Week 3.

tasks.title: Allow SSH from your IP only
tasks.objective: Add one inbound rule allowing SSH from your own address, then prove it is allowed from you and blocked elsewhere.

steps.title: Add the SSH rule
steps.instruction: Allow TCP 22 from your IP address only.

commands.cmd: MYIP=$(curl -s https://checkip.amazonaws.com); echo $MYIP
commands.explain: Run this on YOUR laptop, not CloudShell: it prints the address your laptop reaches the internet from.

commands.cmd: SG=$(aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters Name=group-name,Values=sg-tools-team01 --query "SecurityGroups[0].GroupId" --output text); aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id $SG --protocol tcp --port 22 --cidr $MYIP/32 --query "SecurityGroupRules[0].CidrIpv4" --output text
commands.explain: A /32 is exactly one address.

steps.whatItMeans: Never 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22: bots scan the whole internet for open SSH within minutes.

steps.title: Test allowed and blocked
steps.description: SSH connects from your laptop and times out from CloudShell.
steps.instruction: Test SSH from your laptop, then from CloudShell.
instructionList: Start the instance: EC2 → Instances → ec2-tools-team01 → Start.
From your laptop: ssh -i kp-team01.pem ec2-user@PUBLIC_IP — expect a prompt.
From CloudShell: the same command — expect a timeout.
Stop the instance when done.
steps.expectedOutput: SSH connects from your laptop and times out from CloudShell.
steps.whatItMeans: A rule is only proved when something that should fail does fail.

fixes.fix: Your IP changed (Wi-Fi, VPN). Re-run the first command and add the new address.

steps.title: Record it in the Solution Architecture Document
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Solution Architecture Document.
instructionList: One allowed row, one blocked row.
steps.whatItMeans: Week 6 removes this rule entirely; this record is the before.

tasks.title: Create the DynamoDB table
tasks.objective: Create an on-demand DynamoDB table and seed the counter item.

steps.title: Create the table
steps.instruction: Create an on-demand table keyed on id.

commands.cmd: aws dynamodb create-table --table-name capstone-team01-visitors --attribute-definitions AttributeName=id,AttributeType=S --key-schema AttributeName=id,KeyType=HASH --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST --tags Key=owner,Value=team01-infra --query TableDescription.TableStatus --output text
commands.explain: On-demand bills per request, so an idle counter costs nothing.

commands.cmd: aws dynamodb wait table-exists --table-name capstone-team01-visitors && echo ACTIVE
commands.explain: Waits until the table can take writes.

steps.whatItMeans: Provisioned capacity would charge every hour even when nobody visits.

steps.title: Seed the counter
steps.instruction: Put the item { id: site, count: 0 }.

commands.cmd: aws dynamodb put-item --table-name capstone-team01-visitors --item '{"id":{"S":"site"},"count":{"N":"0"}}' && aws dynamodb get-item --table-name capstone-team01-visitors --key '{"id":{"S":"site"}}' --output text
commands.explain: DynamoDB types every value: S for string, N for number.

steps.whatItMeans: The Lambda updates this one item.

steps.title: Record it in the Application & API Design Specification
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Application & API Design Specification.
instructionList: Table name, partition key, the seed item.
steps.whatItMeans: The API spec’s data model.

tasks.title: Build the counter Lambda and API
tasks.objective: Create a Lambda that atomically adds one to the counter, put an HTTP API in front, and show the count on the site.

steps.title: Create the function
steps.description: The function exists; a Test event returns a count.
steps.instruction: Create a Python Lambda that adds one to the count.
instructionList: Name capstone-team01-counter, Python 3.12, create a new basic execution role.
Code: update_item with UpdateExpression "ADD #c :one", ReturnValues UPDATED_NEW. Deploy.
Configuration → Environment variables: TABLE_NAME = capstone-team01-visitors.
steps.expectedOutput: The function exists; a Test event returns a count.
steps.whatItMeans: ADD is atomic: two visitors at once both count. The Test fails until the role may write the table — next step.

steps.title: Let it write the table, add the API
steps.description: The trigger is listed with an https://….execute-api… endpoint.
steps.where: Lambda → Configuration → Permissions, then Add trigger
steps.instruction: Grant the table, then add an HTTP API trigger.
instructionList: Role → Add permissions → Create inline policy: dynamodb:UpdateItem on the table’s ARN only.
Add trigger → API Gateway → Create HTTP API, security Open.
Copy the API endpoint.
steps.expectedOutput: The trigger is listed with an https://….execute-api… endpoint.
steps.whatItMeans: The role names one action on one table. Week 5 checks nothing broader crept in.

steps.title: Call it and show it
steps.instruction: Call the API, then add the count to the page.

commands.cmd: API=https://abc123.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/default/capstone-team01-counter; curl -s $API
commands.explain: Each call adds one. Then add fetch() of this URL to site/index.html, writing the result into #visitor-count, and redeploy.

steps.whatItMeans: The page calls the API from the browser, which is why CORS matters next.

steps.title: Record it in the Application & API Design Specification
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Application & API Design Specification.
instructionList: GET, the path, what it returns, its status codes.
steps.whatItMeans: The spec another developer would call your API from.

tasks.title: Lock CORS and keep secrets out
tasks.objective: Allow only your site to call the API from a browser, prove another origin is refused, and confirm no key exists anywhere.

steps.title: Allow only your site
steps.instruction: Set the API’s CORS to your site only.

commands.cmd: APIID=$(aws apigatewayv2 get-apis --query "Items[?contains(Name, 'capstone-team01')].ApiId | [0]" --output text); SITE=https://d111111abcdef8.cloudfront.net
commands.explain: Set SITE to your own CloudFront URL, no trailing slash.

commands.cmd: aws apigatewayv2 update-api --api-id $APIID --cors-configuration AllowOrigins=$SITE,AllowMethods=GET --query CorsConfiguration
commands.explain: Browsers only let pages from listed origins read the API’s answers.

steps.whatItMeans: Never "*": a wildcard lets any website use your API from its visitors’ browsers.

steps.title: Prove a foreign origin is refused
steps.description: Prove a foreign origin is refused
steps.instruction: Call the API as another website would.

commands.cmd: curl -s -D - -o /dev/null -H "Origin: https://evil.example" $API | grep -i access-control || echo "no CORS header — refused"
commands.explain: A foreign origin gets no Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, so its browser discards the answer. Set $API to your endpoint first.

steps.whatItMeans: CORS protects browsers, not the API: curl still gets a count. That is why the API holds no secrets.

steps.title: Confirm there is no key
steps.description: No key anywhere; the function reaches the table through its role.
steps.instruction: Check the page and the function hold no key.
instructionList: View the site source: only the API URL, no key.
Lambda environment variables: only TABLE_NAME. Access comes from the role.
steps.expectedOutput: No key anywhere; the function reaches the table through its role.
steps.whatItMeans: An IAM role hands out short-lived credentials automatically — there is nothing to leak.

steps.title: Record it in the Application & API Design Specification
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Application & API Design Specification.
instructionList: The allowed origin, the negative test, where access comes from.
steps.whatItMeans: The first line of the secrets register.

commands.sample:

Amazon Simple Storage Service	0.01

tasks.title: Alarm on Lambda errors
tasks.objective: Create an SNS topic and a CloudWatch alarm that emails when the function errors.
definitionOfDone: The alarm exists and emails the team

steps.title: Create the topic
steps.instruction: Create an SNS topic that emails the team.

commands.cmd: TOPIC=$(aws sns create-topic --name capstone-team01-alerts --query TopicArn --output text); aws sns subscribe --topic-arn $TOPIC --protocol email --notification-endpoint team01-alerts@school.edu --query SubscriptionArn --output text
commands.explain: Confirm the subscription from the email AWS sends, or nothing is delivered.

steps.whatItMeans: One topic, many alarms: change the email once.

steps.title: Create the alarm
steps.instruction: Alarm when Errors is above zero in five minutes.

commands.cmd: aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name capstone-team01-counter-errors --namespace AWS/Lambda --metric-name Errors --dimensions Name=FunctionName,Value=capstone-team01-counter --statistic Sum --period 300 --evaluation-periods 1 --threshold 0 --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold --treat-missing-data notBreaching --alarm-actions $TOPIC && aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names capstone-team01-counter-errors --query "MetricAlarms[0].StateValue" --output text
commands.explain: Any error in five minutes fires it. Missing data (no traffic) is treated as fine.

steps.whatItMeans: Errors are the signal users feel.

steps.title: Record it in the Monitoring & Incident Report
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Monitoring & Incident Report.
instructionList: The signal, where it is measured, the threshold, the action.
steps.whatItMeans: The monitoring half of the incident report.

tasks.title: Find a failure in CloudWatch Logs
tasks.objective: Break the function on purpose, find the error in CloudWatch Logs, and restore it.

steps.title: Break it
steps.instruction: Point the function at a table that does not exist.

commands.cmd: aws lambda update-function-configuration --function-name capstone-team01-counter --environment "Variables={TABLE_NAME=capstone-team01-missing}" --query LastUpdateStatus --output text
commands.explain: The API now returns 500. Load the site twice to generate errors.

steps.whatItMeans: Breaking it yourself means you know the answer, so you can learn the tool that finds it.

steps.title: Find it
steps.instruction: Read the latest errors from the log group.

commands.cmd: aws logs filter-log-events --log-group-name /aws/lambda/capstone-team01-counter --filter-pattern ERROR --max-items 2 --query "events[].message" --output text
commands.explain: Every Lambda writes to a log group named after it.

steps.whatItMeans: The exception names the layer — configuration — before you open any code.

steps.title: Restore it
steps.instruction: Put the right table name back and retest.

commands.cmd: aws lambda update-function-configuration --function-name capstone-team01-counter --environment "Variables={TABLE_NAME=capstone-team01-visitors}" -o none; sleep 5; curl -s $API
commands.explain: Set $API to your endpoint. A count means it is fixed.

steps.whatItMeans: A fix is not done until the retest passes.

steps.title: Record it in the Monitoring & Incident Report
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Monitoring & Incident Report.
instructionList: Add a signal row for errors in CloudWatch Logs.
steps.whatItMeans: Your half of the monitoring table.

tasks.title: Work one incident layer by layer
tasks.objective: Break CORS on purpose, then work it as an incident: symptom, layer, evidence, root cause, fix, prevention.
definitionOfDone: An incident record with all six parts

steps.title: Inject the fault
steps.instruction: Replace the allowed origin with a wrong one.

commands.cmd: APIID=$(aws apigatewayv2 get-apis --query "Items[?contains(Name, 'capstone-team01')].ApiId | [0]" --output text); aws apigatewayv2 update-api --api-id $APIID --cors-configuration AllowOrigins=https://wrong.example,AllowMethods=GET --query CorsConfiguration.AllowOrigins
commands.explain: The page still loads, but its script can no longer read the count.

steps.whatItMeans: A realistic fault: nothing is “down”, one feature silently stops.

steps.title: Find the layer
steps.description: The console names CORS as the cause.
steps.instruction: Follow the symptom down the layers.
instructionList: Symptom: the count is missing.
Network tab: the API answered 200 — the network and the function work.
Console: “blocked by CORS policy” — the configuration layer.
steps.expectedOutput: The console names CORS as the cause.
steps.whatItMeans: Working down the layers stops you fixing what is not broken.

steps.title: Fix and retest
steps.instruction: Put your site back and reload.

commands.cmd: aws apigatewayv2 update-api --api-id $APIID --cors-configuration AllowOrigins=https://d111111abcdef8.cloudfront.net,AllowMethods=GET --query CorsConfiguration.AllowOrigins
commands.explain: Use your own CloudFront URL. Reload the site: the count returns.

steps.whatItMeans: Week 10 puts CORS in the template, so drift like this is corrected by the next deploy.

steps.title: Record it in the Monitoring & Incident Report
steps.instruction: Fill your section of the Monitoring & Incident Report.
instructionList: Symptom, layer, evidence, root cause, fix, prevention.
steps.whatItMeans: Week 12 runs this loop again under time pressure.

full.name: template.yaml
full.text:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Description: Capstone IT Services company - the whole environment, as code.

Parameters:
  TeamId:
    Type: String
    AllowedPattern: '^[a-z0-9]{3,8}$'
    Description: Your team, lowercase, e.g. team01. Goes into every name.
  Environment:
    Type: String
    AllowedValues: [dev, prod]
    Default: dev
  OwnerTag:
    Type: String
    Description: Who answers for these resources. Checked by the Week 11 required-tags rule.
  AlertEmail:
    Type: String
    Description: Where the budget and the error alarm send email.
  InstanceType:
    Type: String
    Default: t3.micro
    AllowedValues: [t3.micro, t2.micro]
  LatestAmiId:
    Type: 'AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<AWS::EC2::Image::Id>'
    Default: /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64
    Description: Always the current Amazon Linux 2023 image - no AMI id to look up.
  BudgetAmount:
    Type: Number
    Default: 5
    Description: Monthly budget in USD.
  ThroughWeek:
    Type: Number
    Default: 12
    AllowedValues: [4, 8, 12]
    Description: Deploy the environment as it stands at the end of this week - 4 (Cloud Practitioner), 8 (Solutions Architect) or 12 (everything).

Conditions:
  # Everything from Week 5 on exists only when the deployment reaches that far.
  Week5Plus: !Not [!Equals [!Ref ThroughWeek, 4]]

Resources:
  MonthlyBudget:
    Type: AWS::Budgets::Budget
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 1
        Summary: The $5 guardrail, set before anything can cost money.
    Properties:
      Budget:
        BudgetName: !Sub 'capstone-${TeamId}'
        BudgetType: COST
        TimeUnit: MONTHLY
        BudgetLimit:
          Amount: !Ref BudgetAmount
          Unit: USD
      NotificationsWithSubscribers:
        - Notification:
            NotificationType: ACTUAL
            ComparisonOperator: GREATER_THAN
            Threshold: 80
            ThresholdType: PERCENTAGE
          Subscribers:
            - SubscriptionType: EMAIL
              Address: !Ref AlertEmail

  Vpc:
    Type: AWS::EC2::VPC
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 1
        Summary: The company network.
    Properties:
      CidrBlock: 10.10.0.0/16
      EnableDnsSupport: true
      EnableDnsHostnames: true
      Tags:
        - { Key: Name, Value: !Sub 'vpc-capstone-${TeamId}' }
        - { Key: project, Value: capstone }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  InternetGateway:
    Type: AWS::EC2::InternetGateway
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 1
        Summary: The VPC's door to the internet.
    Properties:
      Tags:
        - { Key: Name, Value: !Sub 'igw-capstone-${TeamId}' }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  GatewayAttachment:
    Type: AWS::EC2::VPCGatewayAttachment
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 1
        Summary: Hangs the internet gateway on the VPC.
    Properties:
      VpcId: !Ref Vpc
      InternetGatewayId: !Ref InternetGateway

  PublicSubnet:
    Type: AWS::EC2::Subnet
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 1
        Summary: The public subnet - its route table points at the internet gateway.
    Properties:
      VpcId: !Ref Vpc
      CidrBlock: 10.10.1.0/24
      AvailabilityZone: !Select [0, !GetAZs '']
      MapPublicIpOnLaunch: true
      Tags:
        - { Key: Name, Value: !Sub 'snet-public-${TeamId}' }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  PublicRouteTable:
    Type: AWS::EC2::RouteTable
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 1
        Summary: Routes for the public subnet.
    Properties:
      VpcId: !Ref Vpc
      Tags:
        - { Key: Name, Value: !Sub 'rt-public-${TeamId}' }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  PublicDefaultRoute:
    Type: AWS::EC2::Route
    DependsOn: GatewayAttachment
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 1
        Summary: Everything not local goes to the internet gateway.
    Properties:
      RouteTableId: !Ref PublicRouteTable
      DestinationCidrBlock: 0.0.0.0/0
      GatewayId: !Ref InternetGateway

  PublicSubnetRouteAssoc:
    Type: AWS::EC2::SubnetRouteTableAssociation
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 1
        Summary: Makes the public subnet use the public route table.
    Properties:
      SubnetId: !Ref PublicSubnet
      RouteTableId: !Ref PublicRouteTable

  ToolsSecurityGroup:
    Type: AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 1
        Summary: The instance's firewall - no inbound rule at all; admin is Session Manager.
    Properties:
      GroupDescription: IT tools server - no inbound, admin through Session Manager
      VpcId: !Ref Vpc
      SecurityGroupEgress:
        - IpProtocol: '-1'
          CidrIp: 0.0.0.0/0
          Description: Outbound for patches and the SSM agent
      Tags:
        - { Key: Name, Value: !Sub 'sg-tools-${TeamId}' }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  PrivateSubnet:
    Type: AWS::EC2::Subnet
    Condition: Week5Plus
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 6
        Summary: The private subnet - no route to the internet gateway.
    Properties:
      VpcId: !Ref Vpc
      CidrBlock: 10.10.2.0/24
      AvailabilityZone: !Select [0, !GetAZs '']
      MapPublicIpOnLaunch: false
      Tags:
        - { Key: Name, Value: !Sub 'snet-private-${TeamId}' }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  PrivateRouteTable:
    Type: AWS::EC2::RouteTable
    Condition: Week5Plus
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 6
        Summary: Routes for the private subnet - local only.
    Properties:
      VpcId: !Ref Vpc
      Tags:
        - { Key: Name, Value: !Sub 'rt-private-${TeamId}' }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  PrivateSubnetRouteAssoc:
    Type: AWS::EC2::SubnetRouteTableAssociation
    Condition: Week5Plus
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 6
        Summary: Makes the private subnet use the private route table.
    Properties:
      SubnetId: !Ref PrivateSubnet
      RouteTableId: !Ref PrivateRouteTable

  InstanceRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Condition: Week5Plus
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 6
        Summary: Lets the instance talk to Session Manager - replaces SSH.
    Properties:
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: ec2.amazonaws.com }
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
      ManagedPolicyArns:
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::aws:policy/AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore'

  InstanceProfile:
    Type: AWS::IAM::InstanceProfile
    Condition: Week5Plus
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 6
        Summary: Carries the instance role onto the instance.
    Properties:
      Roles: [!Ref InstanceRole]

  ToolsInstance:
    Type: AWS::EC2::Instance
    DependsOn: PublicDefaultRoute
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 2
        Summary: The internal IT tools server - Amazon Linux 2023, IMDSv2, encrypted disk.
    Properties:
      ImageId: !Ref LatestAmiId
      InstanceType: !Ref InstanceType
      SubnetId: !Ref PublicSubnet
      SecurityGroupIds: [!Ref ToolsSecurityGroup]
      IamInstanceProfile: !If [Week5Plus, !Ref InstanceProfile, !Ref AWS::NoValue]
      MetadataOptions:
        HttpTokens: required
      BlockDeviceMappings:
        - DeviceName: /dev/xvda
          Ebs:
            VolumeSize: 8
            VolumeType: gp3
            Encrypted: true
      UserData:
        Fn::Base64: |
          #!/bin/bash
          dnf install -y nginx
          echo 'IT tools server OK' > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
          systemctl enable --now nginx
      Tags:
        - { Key: Name, Value: !Sub 'ec2-tools-${TeamId}' }
        - { Key: project, Value: capstone }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  DataVolume:
    Type: AWS::EC2::Volume
    Condition: Week5Plus
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 7
        Summary: The instance's second disk, for data that must outlive the OS.
    Properties:
      AvailabilityZone: !GetAtt ToolsInstance.AvailabilityZone
      Size: 8
      VolumeType: gp3
      Encrypted: true
      Tags:
        - { Key: Name, Value: !Sub 'ebs-data-tools-${TeamId}' }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  DataVolumeAttachment:
    Type: AWS::EC2::VolumeAttachment
    Condition: Week5Plus
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 7
        Summary: Plugs the data volume into the instance.
    Properties:
      InstanceId: !Ref ToolsInstance
      VolumeId: !Ref DataVolume
      Device: /dev/sdf

  SiteBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 2
        Summary: Holds the website files - private, encrypted, versioned (Week 8).
    Properties:
      PublicAccessBlockConfiguration:
        BlockPublicAcls: true
        BlockPublicPolicy: true
        IgnorePublicAcls: true
        RestrictPublicBuckets: true
      OwnershipControls:
        Rules:
          - ObjectOwnership: BucketOwnerEnforced
      BucketEncryption:
        ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration:
          - ServerSideEncryptionByDefault:
              SSEAlgorithm: AES256
      VersioningConfiguration:
        Status: Enabled
      Tags:
        - { Key: project, Value: capstone }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  SiteOac:
    Type: AWS::CloudFront::OriginAccessControl
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 2
        Summary: The identity CloudFront uses to read the private bucket.
    Properties:
      OriginAccessControlConfig:
        Name: !Sub 'capstone-${TeamId}-site-oac'
        OriginAccessControlOriginType: s3
        SigningBehavior: always
        SigningProtocol: sigv4

  SiteDistribution:
    Type: AWS::CloudFront::Distribution
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 2
        Summary: Serves the site over HTTPS worldwide - the S3 website endpoint alone is HTTP only.
    Properties:
      DistributionConfig:
        Enabled: true
        DefaultRootObject: index.html
        HttpVersion: http2
        PriceClass: PriceClass_100
        Origins:
          - Id: s3-site
            DomainName: !GetAtt SiteBucket.RegionalDomainName
            OriginAccessControlId: !GetAtt SiteOac.Id
            S3OriginConfig:
              OriginAccessIdentity: ''
        DefaultCacheBehavior:
          TargetOriginId: s3-site
          ViewerProtocolPolicy: redirect-to-https
          CachePolicyId: 658327ea-f89d-4fab-a63d-7e88639e58f6
          Compress: true
      Tags:
        - { Key: project, Value: capstone }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  SiteBucketPolicy:
    Type: AWS::S3::BucketPolicy
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 2
        Summary: Lets exactly one CloudFront distribution read the bucket - nobody else.
    Properties:
      Bucket: !Ref SiteBucket
      PolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Sid: AllowThisDistributionOnly
            Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: cloudfront.amazonaws.com }
            Action: s3:GetObject
            Resource: !Sub '${SiteBucket.Arn}/*'
            Condition:
              StringEquals:
                AWS:SourceArn: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:cloudfront::${AWS::AccountId}:distribution/${SiteDistribution}'

  VisitorTable:
    Type: AWS::DynamoDB::Table
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 3
        Summary: Holds the visitor counter item (id count1). Point-in-time recovery from Week 8.
    Properties:
      BillingMode: PAY_PER_REQUEST
      AttributeDefinitions:
        - AttributeName: id
          AttributeType: S
      KeySchema:
        - AttributeName: id
          KeyType: HASH
      SSESpecification:
        SSEEnabled: true
      PointInTimeRecoverySpecification:
        PointInTimeRecoveryEnabled: true
      Tags:
        - { Key: project, Value: capstone }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  TableNameParameter:
    Type: AWS::SSM::Parameter
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 3
        Summary: Publishes the table name in Parameter Store - configuration, not a secret.
    Properties:
      Name: !Sub '/capstone/${TeamId}/visitor/table'
      Type: String
      Value: !Ref VisitorTable

  CounterFunctionRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 3
        Summary: The Lambda's permissions - write its logs, update ONE table, nothing else.
    Properties:
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: lambda.amazonaws.com }
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
      ManagedPolicyArns:
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole'
      Policies:
        - PolicyName: count-visitors
          PolicyDocument:
            Version: '2012-10-17'
            Statement:
              - Effect: Allow
                Action: [dynamodb:UpdateItem, dynamodb:GetItem]
                Resource: !GetAtt VisitorTable.Arn

  CounterFunction:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Function
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 3
        Summary: The visitor-counter code - one atomic update per visit.
    Properties:
      FunctionName: !Sub 'capstone-${TeamId}-counter'
      Runtime: python3.12
      Handler: index.handler
      Role: !GetAtt CounterFunctionRole.Arn
      Timeout: 5
      MemorySize: 128
      Environment:
        Variables:

      Code:
        ZipFile: |
          import json, os, boto3
          table = boto3.resource("dynamodb").Table(os.environ["TABLE_NAME"])

          def handler(event, context):
              r = table.update_item(
                  Key={"id": "count1"},
                  UpdateExpression="ADD #c :one",
                  ExpressionAttributeNames={"#c": "count"},
                  ExpressionAttributeValues={":one": 1},
                  ReturnValues="UPDATED_NEW",
              )
              return {
                  "statusCode": 200,
                  "headers": {"Content-Type": "application/json"},
                  "body": json.dumps({"count": int(r["Attributes"]["count"])}),

        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  ApiIntegration:
    Type: AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Integration
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 3
        Summary: Connects the API to the Lambda function.
    Properties:
      ApiId: !Ref HttpApi
      IntegrationType: AWS_PROXY
      IntegrationUri: !GetAtt CounterFunction.Arn
      PayloadFormatVersion: '2.0'

  ApiRoute:
    Type: AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Route
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 3
        Summary: GET /count goes to the integration.
    Properties:
      ApiId: !Ref HttpApi
      RouteKey: GET /count
      Target: !Sub 'integrations/${ApiIntegration}'

  ApiStage:
    Type: AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Stage
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 3
        Summary: The default stage - changes deploy automatically.
    Properties:
      ApiId: !Ref HttpApi
      StageName: $default
      AutoDeploy: true

  ApiInvokePermission:
    Type: AWS::Lambda::Permission
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 3
        Summary: Lets this API - and only this route - invoke the function.
    Properties:
      Action: lambda:InvokeFunction
      FunctionName: !Ref CounterFunction
      Principal: apigateway.amazonaws.com
      SourceArn: !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:execute-api:${AWS::Region}:${AWS::AccountId}:${HttpApi}/*/*/count'

  CounterLogGroup:
    Type: AWS::Logs::LogGroup
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 4
        Summary: Where the function's logs land - kept two weeks.
    Properties:
      LogGroupName: !Sub '/aws/lambda/capstone-${TeamId}-counter'
      RetentionInDays: 14

  AlertTopic:
    Type: AWS::SNS::Topic
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 4
        Summary: Who gets told when an alarm fires.
    Properties:
      TopicName: !Sub 'capstone-${TeamId}-alerts'

    Metadata:

      Statistic: Sum

      EvaluationPeriods: 1

      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanThreshold
      TreatMissingData: notBreaching

  ReadOnlyGroup:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Group
    Condition: Week5Plus
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 5
        Summary: An IAM group that can look at everything and change nothing.
    Properties:
      ManagedPolicyArns:
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::aws:policy/ReadOnlyAccess'

starter.text:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Description: Capstone IT Services company - the whole environment, as code.

Parameters:
  TeamId:
    Type: String
    AllowedPattern: '^[a-z0-9]{3,8}$'
    Description: Your team, lowercase, e.g. team01. Goes into every name.
  Environment:
    Type: String
    AllowedValues: [dev, prod]
    Default: dev
  OwnerTag:
    Type: String
    Description: Who answers for these resources. Checked by the Week 11 required-tags rule.
  AlertEmail:
    Type: String
    Description: Where the budget and the error alarm send email.
  InstanceType:
    Type: String
    Default: "FILL-ME: the free-tier instance type"
    AllowedValues: [t3.micro, t2.micro]
  LatestAmiId:
    Type: 'AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<AWS::EC2::Image::Id>'
    Default: /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64
    Description: Always the current Amazon Linux 2023 image - no AMI id to look up.
  BudgetAmount:
    Type: Number
    Default: 5
    Description: Monthly budget in USD.
  ThroughWeek:
    Type: Number
    Default: 12
    AllowedValues: [4, 8, 12]
    Description: Deploy the environment as it stands at the end of this week - 4 (Cloud Practitioner), 8 (Solutions Architect) or 12 (everything).

Conditions:
  # Everything from Week 5 on exists only when the deployment reaches that far.
  Week5Plus: !Not [!Equals [!Ref ThroughWeek, 4]]

Resources:
  MonthlyBudget:
    Type: AWS::Budgets::Budget
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 1
        Summary: The $5 guardrail, set before anything can cost money.
    Properties:
      Budget:
        BudgetName: !Sub 'capstone-${TeamId}'
        BudgetType: COST
        TimeUnit: MONTHLY
        BudgetLimit:
          Amount: !Ref BudgetAmount
          Unit: USD
      NotificationsWithSubscribers:
        - Notification:
            NotificationType: ACTUAL
            ComparisonOperator: GREATER_THAN
            Threshold: 80
            ThresholdType: PERCENTAGE
          Subscribers:
            - SubscriptionType: EMAIL
              Address: !Ref AlertEmail

  Vpc:
    Type: AWS::EC2::VPC
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 1
        Summary: The company network.
    Properties:
      CidrBlock: "FILL-ME: the VPC address space"
      EnableDnsSupport: true
      EnableDnsHostnames: true
      Tags:
        - { Key: Name, Value: !Sub 'vpc-capstone-${TeamId}' }
        - { Key: project, Value: capstone }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  InternetGateway:
    Type: AWS::EC2::InternetGateway
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 1
        Summary: The VPC's door to the internet.
    Properties:
      Tags:
        - { Key: Name, Value: !Sub 'igw-capstone-${TeamId}' }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  GatewayAttachment:
    Type: AWS::EC2::VPCGatewayAttachment
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 1
        Summary: Hangs the internet gateway on the VPC.
    Properties:
      VpcId: !Ref Vpc
      InternetGatewayId: !Ref InternetGateway

  PublicSubnet:
    Type: AWS::EC2::Subnet
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 1
        Summary: The public subnet - its route table points at the internet gateway.
    Properties:
      VpcId: !Ref Vpc
      CidrBlock: "FILL-ME: the public subnet range"
      AvailabilityZone: !Select [0, !GetAZs '']
      MapPublicIpOnLaunch: true
      Tags:
        - { Key: Name, Value: !Sub 'snet-public-${TeamId}' }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  PublicRouteTable:
    Type: AWS::EC2::RouteTable
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 1
        Summary: Routes for the public subnet.
    Properties:
      VpcId: !Ref Vpc
      Tags:
        - { Key: Name, Value: !Sub 'rt-public-${TeamId}' }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  PublicDefaultRoute:
    Type: AWS::EC2::Route
    DependsOn: GatewayAttachment
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 1
        Summary: Everything not local goes to the internet gateway.
    Properties:
      RouteTableId: !Ref PublicRouteTable
      DestinationCidrBlock: 0.0.0.0/0
      GatewayId: !Ref InternetGateway

  PublicSubnetRouteAssoc:
    Type: AWS::EC2::SubnetRouteTableAssociation
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 1
        Summary: Makes the public subnet use the public route table.
    Properties:
      SubnetId: !Ref PublicSubnet
      RouteTableId: !Ref PublicRouteTable

  ToolsSecurityGroup:
    Type: AWS::EC2::SecurityGroup
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 1
        Summary: The instance's firewall - no inbound rule at all; admin is Session Manager.
    Properties:
      GroupDescription: IT tools server - no inbound, admin through Session Manager
      VpcId: !Ref Vpc
      SecurityGroupEgress:
        - IpProtocol: '-1'
          CidrIp: 0.0.0.0/0
          Description: Outbound for patches and the SSM agent
      Tags:
        - { Key: Name, Value: !Sub 'sg-tools-${TeamId}' }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  PrivateSubnet:
    Type: AWS::EC2::Subnet
    Condition: Week5Plus
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 6
        Summary: The private subnet - no route to the internet gateway.
    Properties:
      VpcId: !Ref Vpc
      CidrBlock: "FILL-ME: the private subnet range"
      AvailabilityZone: !Select [0, !GetAZs '']
      MapPublicIpOnLaunch: false
      Tags:
        - { Key: Name, Value: !Sub 'snet-private-${TeamId}' }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  PrivateRouteTable:
    Type: AWS::EC2::RouteTable
    Condition: Week5Plus
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 6
        Summary: Routes for the private subnet - local only.
    Properties:
      VpcId: !Ref Vpc
      Tags:
        - { Key: Name, Value: !Sub 'rt-private-${TeamId}' }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  PrivateSubnetRouteAssoc:

    Condition: Week5Plus
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 6
        Summary: Makes the private subnet use the private route table.
    Properties:
      SubnetId: !Ref PrivateSubnet
      RouteTableId: !Ref PrivateRouteTable

  InstanceRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Condition: Week5Plus
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 6
        Summary: Lets the instance talk to Session Manager - replaces SSH.
    Properties:
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument:
        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:
          - Effect: Allow
            Principal: { Service: ec2.amazonaws.com }
            Action: sts:AssumeRole
      ManagedPolicyArns:
        - !Sub 'arn:${AWS::Partition}:iam::aws:policy/AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore'

  InstanceProfile:
    Type: AWS::IAM::InstanceProfile
    Condition: Week5Plus
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 6
        Summary: Carries the instance role onto the instance.
    Properties:
      Roles: [!Ref InstanceRole]

  ToolsInstance:
    Type: AWS::EC2::Instance
    DependsOn: PublicDefaultRoute
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 2
        Summary: The internal IT tools server - Amazon Linux 2023, IMDSv2, encrypted disk.
    Properties:
      ImageId: !Ref LatestAmiId
      InstanceType: !Ref InstanceType
      SubnetId: !Ref PublicSubnet
      SecurityGroupIds: [!Ref ToolsSecurityGroup]
      IamInstanceProfile: !If [Week5Plus, !Ref InstanceProfile, !Ref AWS::NoValue]
      MetadataOptions:
        HttpTokens: required
      BlockDeviceMappings:
        - DeviceName: /dev/xvda
          Ebs:
            VolumeSize: 8
            VolumeType: gp3
            Encrypted: true
      UserData:
        Fn::Base64: |
          #!/bin/bash
          dnf install -y nginx
          echo 'IT tools server OK' > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
          systemctl enable --now nginx
      Tags:
        - { Key: Name, Value: !Sub 'ec2-tools-${TeamId}' }
        - { Key: project, Value: capstone }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  DataVolume:
    Type: AWS::EC2::Volume
    Condition: Week5Plus
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 7
        Summary: The instance's second disk, for data that must outlive the OS.
    Properties:
      AvailabilityZone: !GetAtt ToolsInstance.AvailabilityZone
      Size: 8
      VolumeType: gp3
      Encrypted: true
      Tags:
        - { Key: Name, Value: !Sub 'ebs-data-tools-${TeamId}' }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  DataVolumeAttachment:
    Type: AWS::EC2::VolumeAttachment
    Condition: Week5Plus
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 7
        Summary: Plugs the data volume into the instance.
    Properties:
      InstanceId: !Ref ToolsInstance
      VolumeId: !Ref DataVolume
      Device: /dev/sdf

  SiteBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 2
        Summary: Holds the website files - private, encrypted, versioned (Week 8).
    Properties:
      PublicAccessBlockConfiguration:
        BlockPublicAcls: true
        BlockPublicPolicy: true
        IgnorePublicAcls: true
        RestrictPublicBuckets: true
      OwnershipControls:
        Rules:
          - ObjectOwnership: BucketOwnerEnforced
      BucketEncryption:
        ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration:
          - ServerSideEncryptionByDefault:

      VersioningConfiguration:
        Status: Enabled
      Tags:
        - { Key: project, Value: capstone }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  SiteOac:
    Type: AWS::CloudFront::OriginAccessControl
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 2
        Summary: The identity CloudFront uses to read the private bucket.
    Properties:
      OriginAccessControlConfig:
        Name: !Sub 'capstone-${TeamId}-site-oac'
        OriginAccessControlOriginType: s3
        SigningBehavior: always
        SigningProtocol: sigv4

  SiteDistribution:
    Type: AWS::CloudFront::Distribution
    Metadata:
      Capstone:
        Week: 2
        Summary: Serves the site over HTTPS worldwide - the S3 website endpoint alone is HTTP only.
    Properties:
      DistributionConfig:
        Enabled: true
        DefaultRootObject: index.html
        HttpVersion: http2
        PriceClass: PriceClass_100
        Origins:

            OriginAccessControlId: !GetAtt SiteOac.Id
            S3OriginConfig:

        DefaultCacheBehavior:

          ViewerProtocolPolicy: "FILL-ME: what happens to plain HTTP"
          CachePolicyId: 658327ea-f89d-4fab-a63d-7e88639e58f6
          Compress: true
      Tags:
        - { Key: project, Value: capstone }
        - { Key: owner, Value: !Ref OwnerTag }

  SiteBucketPolicy:

        Version: '2012-10-17'
        Statement:

            Action: s3:GetObject

CUSTODY_RULES: Preserve the original — work on copies; never edit or rename the original artifact after collection.
Name every artifact `YYYYMMDD_TeamXX_Tool_Action.ext` so it is dated, attributed and self-describing.
Hash on collection: `sha256sum <file> >> Evidence_Hashes.txt`. Verify on receipt/before reporting: `sha256sum -c Evidence_Hashes.txt`.
Log every artifact in this file the moment it is collected — and log every hand-off (who → who, when).
Keep every artifact for a week in `~/team-artifacts/week-N/`; the team package gathers them into `04_Testing_and_Findings/Evidence/`. Keep originals read-only and backed up.
One custodian holds the evidence at a time; record each transfer so the chain is unbroken.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The terminal doesn’t recognise the program — usually a typo or the tool isn’t installed.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Check the spelling. If it’s really missing, install it: sudo apt update && sudo apt install <tool>

variants.otherwise: — the step that first uses a tool says how to install it.

ERROR_ROWS.fix: Add sudo in front on Linux (sudo <command>). On Windows/PowerShell, close it and reopen with “Run as administrator”.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: Connection refused / No route to host / host seems down
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: You can’t reach the target — it’s off, the IP is wrong, or you’re not on the right network.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: ping the address first. Confirm the machine is powered on and that you are on the same subnet as it

variants.then: , and that you set the right IP in Lab access.
variants.otherwise: — a host in another zone only answers once the route between them exists.

variants.then: For nmap, add -Pn to scan a host that blocks ping.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: You’re in the wrong folder, or the path/filename is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run pwd to see where you are and cd ~ to go home.

variants.then: For hydra, rockyou is gzipped by default — unzip it once: sudo gunzip /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt.gz
variants.otherwise: Check the file really exists with ls before you edit it — a config path is easy to mistype.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: That’s a placeholder, not a real address — you copied it literally.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Open the Lab access panel at the top of the Tasks tab and enter {label}; the site then fills it into every command automatically.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: ssh: connect to host … Operation timed out (from home)
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: Your laptop is not on the tailnet, or the host is not.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Check the Tailscale client is signed in and connected on your laptop, then run tailscale status on the host — it must list the host as online. On campus you can still reach it on its 10.10.30.T address while you sort this out.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: The Proxmox console times out but SSH works
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The path is fine; the web service or the port is not.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run systemctl status pveproxy --no-pager over SSH. Remember the console is on port 8006 and https, not http — a plain http:// URL simply hangs.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: It worked yesterday and not today
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The host rebooted and something did not come back, or your address changed.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: systemctl is-active tailscaled on the host must read active. The host keeps the same Tailscale address across reboots, so if the address you saved has changed, you are looking at a rebuilt host that was re-authorised as a new device.

ERROR_ROWS.symptom: Permission denied (publickey) after setting up keys
ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The key is not where the server expects it, or the account is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Run ssh -v to see which key is offered, and confirm you are connecting as the right user. Password login is still enabled until Week 4 hardens it, so you have a way back in — use it rather than locking yourself out further.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: The VM cannot reach the Core over the ops network — the second NIC, the VLAN tag or the bridge is wrong.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: On the host, ip -br a must show vmbr9 UP with the team’s 10.20.T.1 address. Inside the VM, the second interface needs its 10.20.T.x address and no gateway. Still nothing: the switch port is not trunking VLAN 20 — the Networking deep-dive owns that.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: Some commands (a bare ping, a large download, a package install) run until you stop them, or they’re waiting on a slow or unreachable host.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Press Ctrl+C to stop it. Re-check reachability (ping), and give a genuinely long job a minute

variants.otherwise: — an OS install or a big apt upgrade takes minutes, not seconds.

ERROR_ROWS.meaning: When anything fails, the error’s last line usually names the real problem.
ERROR_ROWS.fix: Match that line to the rows above. Also double-check you’re on the machine the step’s WHERE chip names — running the right command on the wrong host is the most common cause.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Open a terminal
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: On a Linux desktop, click the black terminal icon or press Ctrl+Alt+T. On a server you reach over SSH, the terminal is the session itself. You type commands here and press Enter to run them.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: The prompt
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: A line ending in $ (or #) is the prompt — it means the terminal is waiting for you. You don’t type the $ itself.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Paste a command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Copy from this site, then in the terminal press Ctrl+Shift+V (plain Ctrl+V often does nothing in a terminal). Right-click → Paste also works.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Run one line at a time
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: When a step shows several numbered commands, run them one by one — paste one, press Enter, wait for it to finish, then the next.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: sudo = run as admin
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: sudo runs a command with admin rights (it may ask for your password — typing shows nothing, that’s normal). On Windows/PowerShell, instead right-click PowerShell → “Run as administrator”.

TERMINAL_BASICS.label: Stop a stuck command
TERMINAL_BASICS.body: Press Ctrl+C to cancel a command that hangs or runs forever (e.g. a ping with no -c limit).

glossary.data.src_ip: The Wazuh search field holding the source address of a network (Suricata) alert — who the traffic came from.
glossary.data.srcip: The Wazuh search field holding the source address of a host alert (logins, web requests). Its network twin is data.src_ip — search both.
glossary.ossec.conf: The Wazuh agent's config file. It names the SOC to report to and any extra log files to ship.
glossary.hydra: A password-guessing tool. In this lab you run it against your own pod so the SOC has a brute-force attack to detect.
glossary.tcpdump: A command-line tool that records network traffic to a .pcap file you can open in Wireshark.
glossary.Wireshark: A traffic viewer. Open a .pcap in it and "Follow HTTP Stream" to read the exact request an attacker sent.
glossary.Kali: The attacker machine in your lab — a Linux build that ships with nmap, nikto, hydra and the rest.
glossary.Proxmox: A hypervisor — an operating system whose job is to run virtual machines. In Server+ you install it on your own server; in the CySA lab it already runs the lab.
glossary.POST: Power-On Self-Test — the hardware check a machine runs the moment you power it on, before any operating system. Beeps and blink codes are POST talking to you.
glossary.DIMM: A memory stick. Which slots they go in is dictated by the motherboard manual, and the wrong slots can stop the machine starting at all.
glossary.ECC: Error-Correcting Code memory — server RAM that detects and fixes single-bit corruption on the fly. Servers use it; desktops usually do not.
glossary.HCL: Hardware Compatibility List — the check that the software you plan to run officially supports the exact hardware you have, before you build on it.
glossary.UEFI: The modern replacement for the old BIOS firmware. Boot mode matters: an OS installed under UEFI will not boot if the firmware is later switched to legacy.
glossary.IOMMU: The chip feature (Intel VT-d / AMD-Vi) that lets a virtual machine be handed a real piece of hardware, like a NIC, as its own.
glossary.VT-x: Intel’s virtualization extensions. Present is not enough — they must be ENABLED in firmware setup, or the hypervisor cannot start a single VM.
glossary.stripe size: How large a chunk of data a RAID array writes to one disk before moving to the next. The default is right for this build.
glossary.IDS: Intrusion Detection System — software that watches traffic and raises an alert when it matches a known attack pattern. Suricata is yours.
glossary.NVD: National Vulnerability Database — the public catalogue you search to find a CVE and its score for a given software version.
glossary.pod: Your team’s pair of machines: one Ubuntu web server and one Windows PC.
glossary.escalate: Pass an alert on for deeper investigation, with the reason written down, instead of closing it yourself.
glossary.SOC: Security Operations Centre — the team (and dashboard) that watches for attacks around the clock.
glossary.SIEM: Security Information and Event Management — software that gathers logs from everywhere and raises alerts. Wazuh is your SIEM.
glossary.IOC: Indicator of Compromise — a clue an attacker leaves behind, like a bad IP address, file name, or hash.
glossary.CVE: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures — a public ID for one specific known software flaw, e.g. CVE-2021-41773.
glossary.CVSS: A 0–10 score for how severe a vulnerability is, so you can rank what to fix first.
glossary.pcap: A 'packet capture' — a saved recording of network traffic you can open in Wireshark.
glossary.SQLi: SQL injection — tricking a website into running database commands it shouldn't, often to steal data.
glossary.WAF: Web Application Firewall — a filter in front of a website that blocks common attacks like SQL injection.
glossary.POA&M: Plan of Action & Milestones — a to-do list for fixing findings: what, who owns it, and by when.
glossary.PTES: Penetration Testing Execution Standard — the agreed steps of a pentest: recon, scan, exploit, report.
glossary.STRIDE: A checklist of threat types: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
glossary.NIC: Network Interface Card — a machine's network connection. On these VMs it's usually named ens18.
glossary.IaC: Infrastructure as Code — describing machines in a text file a tool applies, so the build is repeatable and the file is the record. Terraform or OpenTofu is yours.
glossary.OpenTofu: The open-source fork of Terraform, kept under the Linux Foundation after HashiCorp changed Terraform’s licence in 2023. Same HCL, same providers, same state files; the command is tofu instead of terraform.
glossary.exporter: A small program on a host that publishes its metrics on an HTTP port for Prometheus to collect. node_exporter for Linux, windows_exporter for Windows.
glossary.IPAM: IP Address Management — the tool that holds every subnet and address and who has it, so the plan and reality are the same document. NetBox is yours.
glossary.FIM: File Integrity Monitoring — an agent that hashes important files and alerts when one changes, which is how a tampered config gets noticed.
glossary.cloud-init: The first-boot setup a cloud image runs: hostname, user, keys and addressing handed in from outside, so a clone comes up configured instead of blank.
glossary.DNAT: Destination NAT — the host rewriting where a packet is going. The rule that turns a request to the host’s campus address on port 80 into a request to websrv in the DMZ.
glossary.MASQUERADE: Source NAT behind the host’s own address, so a reply from the campus LAN or the internet comes back to the host and is handed to the guest that asked.
glossary.published port: A port on the host’s campus address that a DNAT rule hands to a VM behind it. Each one is a deliberate hole in the segmentation, and you should be able to say why it exists.
glossary.idempotent: Running it twice gives the same result as running it once. The property that makes a playbook safe to run every night — and why changed=0 on the second run is the proof.
glossary.drift: Reality diverging from what the code says — a change made in the console instead of the repository. terraform plan (tofu plan) detects it; the next apply may undo it.
glossary.dynamic inventory: Ansible asking the hypervisor which hosts exist instead of reading a list someone typed. The list is never out of date because there is no list.
glossary.XDR: Extended Detection and Response — one platform watching endpoints, logs and files across a whole fleet. Wazuh on the Core is the MSP’s.
glossary.verify job: The backup server re-reading a backup, chunk by chunk, to confirm it is restorable before anyone needs it.
glossary.SLO: Service Level Objective — the availability you promise a client, as a number. The SLA is the contract around it.
glossary.SCA: Security Configuration Assessment — checking a machine's settings against a hardening benchmark.
glossary.Rules of Engagement: The written agreement of what you're allowed to test, and when.
glossary.RoE: Rules of Engagement — the written agreement of what you're allowed to test, and when.
glossary.triage: Quickly sorting alerts into real vs noise and deciding what to escalate — like an ER nurse.
glossary.baseline: A record of what 'normal' looks like, so you can spot what's abnormal later.
glossary.chain of custody: A documented trail of who handled each piece of evidence and when — so it holds up as proof.
glossary.agent: A small program installed on each machine that ships its logs to the SOC.
glossary.gate: A checkpoint at the end of a week — finish its required work before the next week unlocks.
glossary.eve.json: The file where Suricata writes its network alerts.
glossary.subnet: A slice of a network sharing an address range, e.g. 10.10.100.x.
glossary.Wazuh: The free, open-source SIEM/SOC platform this lab is built on.
glossary.Suricata: An open-source network intrusion detector that watches traffic and raises alerts.
glossary.Sysmon: A Windows tool that records detailed activity — processes, connections, file changes.
glossary.DVWA: Damn Vulnerable Web App — a deliberately insecure web app used as a safe attack target.
glossary.nmap: A scanner that finds open ports and what software is running on them.
glossary.nikto: A scanner that checks a web server for known issues.
glossary.MITRE ATT&CK: A public catalogue of attacker techniques, used to describe how an attack was carried out.
glossary.MTTD: Mean Time To Detect — the average time from an attack starting to it being noticed.
glossary.MTTR: Mean Time To Respond — the average time from detecting an attack to containing it.
glossary.rule.level: Wazuh scores every alert 0–15 by severity; searching rule.level:>=7 keeps the ones that usually matter.
glossary.rule.groups: The category tags Wazuh puts on an alert (e.g. authentication_failed, ids, web) — handy for filtering by attack type.
glossary.agent.name: The Wazuh field naming which machine an alert came from (e.g. Team07-ubuntu) — use it to filter to one host.
glossary.event channel: A named Windows log stream — Sysmon writes to Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational, which the agent forwards.
glossary.Emerging Threats ruleset: The community alert rules Suricata downloads with suricata-update — without them it sees traffic but raises nothing.
glossary.DQL: Dashboard Query Language — the field:value search syntax in the Wazuh/OpenSearch search bar (e.g. data.src_ip:10.10.30.7).
glossary.Discover: The Wazuh/OpenSearch view that lists raw events in a table you can search, add columns to, and save.
glossary.time picker: The date/time control (top-right) that sets which window of events you see — the #1 reason a correct search looks empty.
glossary.visualization: A saved chart (bar, pie, table) built from a search — the building block you drop onto a dashboard.
glossary.dashboard: A saved page of visualizations and searches you assemble to watch at a glance.
glossary.rule.description: The Wazuh field holding the human-readable name of the rule that fired — useful to group and count alerts by.
glossary.syscheck: Wazuh’s File Integrity Monitoring engine; its events carry syscheck.path and whether a file was added/modified/deleted.
glossary.sensor: A program on a machine that watches activity and reports it to the SOC — your Wazuh agent, Suricata and Sysmon are all sensors.
glossary.endpoint: Any individual computer on the network — a laptop, server or VM — as opposed to the network gear between them.
glossary.telemetry: The stream of activity data a machine sends about itself — processes, logins, connections — that the SOC watches.
glossary.hash: A short fingerprint calculated from a file; change one byte and the fingerprint changes, so it proves the file was not tampered with.
glossary.hashing: Running a file through a formula to get its fixed-length fingerprint (its hash).
glossary.SHA-256: A widely trusted hashing method that turns any file into a 64-character fingerprint.
glossary.false positive: An alert that turned out to be harmless — the tool flagged something that was not actually an attack.
glossary.true positive: An alert that was real — the flagged activity really was malicious.
glossary.enroll: To register a machine with the SOC so its agent starts sending logs.
glossary.brute force: Guessing a password by automatically trying huge numbers of combinations until one works.
glossary.port scan: Probing a machine to list which network ports are open, to discover what services it is running.
glossary.SSH: Secure Shell — a way to log in to and run commands on another machine over the network, from your terminal.
glossary.pivot: To follow a clue (like an IP or username) from one log into related events, tracing an attacker’s movements.
glossary.hardening: Making a machine harder to attack by closing unused services, fixing weak settings and applying updates.
glossary.containment: Stopping an attack from spreading — e.g. isolating the affected machine — once you have detected it.
glossary.vulnerability: A weakness in software or configuration that an attacker could exploit.
glossary.vuln: Short for vulnerability — a weakness an attacker could exploit.
glossary.firewall: A filter that allows or blocks network connections by rule, to keep unwanted traffic out.
glossary.ufw: Uncomplicated Firewall — the simple command-line firewall on Ubuntu (e.g. ufw allow 22).
glossary.VLAN: A virtual LAN — one physical switch split into separate networks. Ports in different VLANs cannot talk without something routing between them, which is the whole point.
glossary.trunk: A link between switches that carries several VLANs at once, tagging each frame with its VLAN id (802.1Q). The alternative is one cable per VLAN.
glossary.native VLAN: The one VLAN a trunk carries UNTAGGED. If the two ends disagree about which it is, traffic silently lands in the wrong network — the classic trunk fault.
glossary.SVI: Switched Virtual Interface — a VLAN’s gateway configured on the switch itself. A switch with SVIs routes between VLANs at wire speed; a switch without them needs a router.
glossary.router-on-a-stick: Inter-VLAN routing done by a router over a single trunk, with one subinterface per VLAN. What you build when the switch cannot route — same outcome, one link carrying all of it.
glossary.EtherChannel: Two or more physical links bundled into one logical link, so a cable can fail without an outage and the bandwidth adds up. LACP is the protocol that negotiates it.
glossary.spanning tree: The protocol that stops a loop when switches have more than one path between them, by blocking all but one. It always picks a root switch — set it deliberately or it picks the oldest one.
glossary.PortFast: Tells spanning tree an access port has a PC on it, not a switch, so it forwards immediately instead of waiting. Never on a port that could reach another switch.
glossary.BPDU Guard: Shuts a PortFast port the moment it hears spanning-tree messages — which means somebody plugged a switch into a desk port. The protection that makes PortFast safe.
glossary.OSPF: A routing protocol: routers tell each other which networks they can reach, so each works out its own routes. It replaces static routes and reacts when a link dies.
glossary.OSPF area: A grouping that limits how far routing detail spreads. This course uses a single area 0 — the backbone — because one correctly adjacent area is the CCNA outcome.
glossary.adjacency: Two OSPF routers that have agreed to exchange routes. It has to reach the FULL state; anything less is the protocol telling you what does not match.
glossary.NAT: Network Address Translation — rewriting addresses as traffic crosses the edge, so internal addresses that mean nothing on the internet can still reach it.
glossary.PAT: Port Address Translation, sometimes "NAT overload" — the whole company sharing one public address, told apart by port number. What almost every small site actually runs.
glossary.ACL: Access Control List — an ordered list of permit and deny rules applied to an interface in one direction. It ends with an implicit deny, which is why the order matters.
glossary.port security: Limits which or how many MAC addresses a switch port accepts, so a stranger plugging into a desk port cannot quietly join the network.
glossary.ip helper-address: Tells a router to forward DHCP requests from a VLAN to a DHCP server somewhere else. The enterprise pattern, versus the router serving DHCP itself.
glossary.SNMP: The protocol a monitoring system uses to read a device’s interfaces, CPU and memory. Read-only is all a NOC needs; v3 is the version with real authentication.
glossary.syslog: Device log messages sent to a central collector. With synchronised clocks it turns "it broke this morning" into a readable sequence across every device.
glossary.NetBox: The source of truth for the network: sites, devices, interfaces, cables, VLANs and prefixes, with an API. It replaces the spreadsheet once the spreadsheet stops scaling.
glossary.Oxidized: Collects every device’s configuration on a schedule and commits it to Git, so you have both a backup and a history of what changed.
glossary.source of truth: The one system that DEFINES what the network should be. Tools read from it and configure devices to match, so the documentation cannot drift from reality.
glossary.PoE: Power over Ethernet — the switch powering the device on the far end of the cable, which is how phones and access points run without a plug of their own.
glossary.SFP: The slot a fibre (or copper) transceiver plugs into, for uplinks that go further or faster than the built-in ports.
